article.para: Computers deal with text in several formats: programming-language code like C or C++, file formats like HTML, XML, JSON, and even user input such as with a shell. These formats have some structure to them, but this structure doesn’t always reflect the way the computer handles the data itself. For example, a JSON object might list a 7-digit number, like 5749175 as the series of digits 5749175, but the computer processing the data might represent that number internally as four bytes with the values 0, 87, 185, and 183.

Parsing is the process of taking the structure of a file format, and converting it to a form the computer can more easily work with. A JSON parser might convert JSON objects to a programming language’s internal structure types, or convert an XML document to a tree structure that represents the structure of the document. Siliko includes a parser that converts a mathemetical notation, closer to one used by people than what a computer might use, into a tree structure that’s easier to process with a computer.

section.title: Lexical Analysis
section.para: When parsing, there are two major steps. The first step is lexical analysis. This step involves the conversion of strings of arbitrary characters to usable units. For example, the string 42 could represent a number, but to the computer, it’s two bytes, with the values 52 and 50. In order for it to be useful as the value 42, a tool called the lexical analyzer determines where the number begins and where it ends, then converts the series of bytes to the useful value 42. Strictly speaking, the series of bytes to be converted is called a lexeme, and the data structure that represents that it’s an integer with a certain value is called a token. However, many programmers will also refer to lexemes as tokens. Because this process converts lexemes to tokens, the process of lexical analysis is also called tokenization, and a lexical analyzer can also be called a tokenizer or a lexer.

A lexical analyzer works by reading input one character at a time, whitling down the possible results as it reads each character until, by its internal rules, it has reached the end of input and narrowed down the possible type of the input to one type. This is done with a tool called a finite-state machine.

A finite-state machine has a set of states representing the possibilities and how far into the process it is. In the Siliko language integers and real numbers both start out with a series of digits, but real numbers also have a decimal point. So, when the lexical analyzer starts processing a new number, for example 12.5 it starts out in a ‘blank’ start state. It then reads the first character, 1. This puts the tokenizer into a state representing “maybe an integer”. It will then read the 2, and continue in the same state. When the analyzer reaches the decimal point, however, it knows that this isn’t an integer but rather a real number. So, it changes state to “real number”. Reading the next character, 5, the lexical analyzer continues in the “real number” state. It then reads the next character, which, presumably is an operator or a space character, and determines that the lexeme is done, and changes to a termination state. Once it has reached a termination state, the lexical analyzer does the final conversion to a useful form, a token representing the type of the data the lexeme represents in the language, in this case a real number, and the value itself in a more convenient form, such as the machine’s internal floating-point representation. The Lexical analyzer then passes this token on to the syntactic analyzer.

section.title: Syntactic Analysis
section.para: Syntactic analysis is the process of reading a series of tokens, provided by the lexical analyser, and converting them to a usable structure, most often a syntax tree. The tool that does this could be called a syntactic analyzer but is often simply called the parser.

This section of the parser takes care of making sense of what the arrangement of the tokens means. For example, an infix parser would look at a sequence of tokens such as “integer with value 2”, “operator +”, and “integer with value 3”, and concludes that such a sequence is an addition operation with operands “integer with value 2” and “integer with value 3”. It will then generate a syntax tree representing the operation such as in .
A syntactic analyzer can read a complex series of tokens and break them down into productions representing these rules. For example, a production for an addition operation might look like .

This reads that an expression is one of two things, either the sequence of a number, followed by a plus sign, followed by another number, or just a number. A number is a sequence of one or more digits. This means that, by these rule, 2 + 3 is an expression, and so is just 2. These rules can be stacked to create a complex grammar indicating the rules and organization of a language. The way these productions are stacked can be used to specify precedence and associativity. For example, if you want to mix addition and multiplication, while making sure that the multiplication takes precedence, you could stack the rules like this.

One will notice each of these productions can have itself as a component. An expression can have another expression as a portion of itself. So, given the expression 2 + 3 + 5 the first expression 2 + 3 is a component of a second expression which has (2 + 3), +, and 5 as its component.

Since each production can simply be the next rule in the list, a term on its own can be an expression, and a number can be a term. This, combined with the above rule allowing for productions within themselves, allows trees to be built respecting the order of operations.

For example, 2 + 3 * 5 would first be read as a number 2, an addition operation, followed by a number, however, as the next operator is multiplication, this is interpreted as a term, and so the 3, *, and 5 will be handled as a term, then passed down to the production for the expression, which takes an expression, which can be a term, which can be a number, which is 2, followed by an addition operator, followed by the term (3 * 5), resulting in a parse tree such as:
A More Complex Parse Tree
+ 2 * 3 5
As can be seen in this parse tree, the 3 * 5 operation is handled separately, and the + operaton can’t be processed before the multiplication operation is handled.
For the complete grammar of the Siliko infix parser, see the Siliko Infix Language Reference.
